title: Aerospace, Aviation & MRO RFID — Part-Level Serialization for ATA Spec 2000 Ch. 9-5 & FAA AC 20-162A
summary: Airframe, engine, rotable and expendable aerospace parts are serialized with UHF and NFC RFID tags that survive the full 30-year airframe service life, comply with ATA Spec 2000 Chapter 9-5 automated identification of parts, FAA AC 20-162A (the FAA's accepted means of automated part identification), SAE AS5678 passive RFID guidance, and EASA ETSO-2C513 where applicable. Proud Tek supplies aircraft-grade on-metal UHF part tags (Murata MAGICSTRAP, NXP UCODE 9, Alien Higgs-9 on ceramic or PPS substrate), NFC life-cycle-data tags for MRO removal history, and the encoded-data service that converts OEM and MRO part-number / serial-number records into ATA Spec 2000-compliant EPC memory layouts.
heroPoints: ATA Spec 2000 Ch. 9-5 & FAA AC 20-162A compliant. Part-level serialization in UHF passive RFID format accepted by the FAA for automated identification of parts (AIP).
30-year airframe service-life rated. UV-stabilized, vibration-qualified, temperature-cycled (-55 to +125 °C) substrates and encapsulation proven across commercial and military programs.
MRO lifecycle-data-ready. NFC NTAG224/216 and UHF UCODE 9 with 128-224 bits of User memory carry removal date, shop visit, AD compliance status on-tag for MRO facility read without backend lookup.

sections.title: Challenges aerospace manufacturers and MRO operators face without RFID
bullets: Paper-based part records and handwritten serial lookup. A typical wide-body heavy-check (C or D check) involves 800-2,000 removals and reinstallations; without automated part identification, each part lookup consumes 3-8 minutes of mechanic time and the check overrun rate from records errors is 12-18%.

Rotable pool traceability: engine shops, wheel-and-brake shops and component shops manage rotable pools of 10,000-50,000 LRUs and MROs where the same part ships, installs, removes, ships back and re-ships multiple times per year; manual serial tracking is the #1 audit finding in FAA Part 145 inspection cycles.

AD compliance verification at incoming inspection. Airworthiness Directives accumulate hundreds per airframe per year; verifying compliance status part-by-part against the maintenance records when a used part arrives at a shop is a 40-60 minute manual task per part that RFID + shop-floor data integration collapses to under 10 seconds.

Counterfeit part ingress: the FAA and EASA both document an ongoing counterfeit parts problem in the aftermarket supply chain; without unit-level cryptographic authentication, a counterfeit bearing, fastener, electronic card or rotable component can enter an MRO shop and be installed on an aircraft.

IUID (Item Unique Identification) for defense-spec aircraft. MIL-STD-130N requires a machine-readable unique identifier on every controlled defense item ≥ $5,000; 2D data matrix meets the mark but does not support line-of-sight-free read required in hangar and flight-line environments.

Tool control in hangar and flight line. Foreign object debris (FOD) from lost tools is a reportable safety incident under FAA and EASA regulations; RFID tool control at shadow board level eliminates FOD risk and satisfies the tool-accountability requirements in FAA Part 145 and military technical orders.

sections.title: How Proud Tek solves aerospace RFID part serialization
bullets: Aircraft-grade on-metal UHF tags. Ceramic or PPS substrate tags (read range 1.5-3 m on metal) using Impinj M730/M750 or NXP UCODE 9 silicon, temperature-cycled -55 to +125 °C, vibration-qualified to RTCA DO-160G and rated for 30-year airframe service life.

ATA Spec 2000 Ch. 9-5 EPC encoding. Tags pre-encoded to the ATA-compliant structure for OEM and MRO part numbers, serial numbers and CAGE code, ready to read by any FAA-accepted AIP reader infrastructure.

NFC lifecycle-data tags for MRO. NTAG224 / NTAG216 with 888 bytes of User memory carry the removal and reinstall history, AD compliance status and shop-visit record directly on the tag so a mechanic can verify part life without network access.

UID / IUID compliant 2D + RFID dual-marking. Combined data-matrix laser mark plus passive UHF RFID on the same nameplate satisfies both MIL-STD-130N visible IUID and FAA AC 20-162A automated identification requirements in a single part mark.

Tool-control UHF tags for shadow boards. Every hand tool in a shadow board or tool crib is tagged with an Impinj M730 UHF hard tag; the board's fixed reader confirms every tool is returned before the mechanic signs off, eliminating FOD risk under FAA Part 145 and military tech-order requirements.

Cryptographic NFC for counterfeit prevention. NTAG424 DNA SUN codes let a receiving MRO shop verify that a part was genuinely manufactured by an approved supplier on the first NFC tap, blocking counterfeit parts at inspection.

faq.question: Is RFID required on aircraft parts?
faq.answer: Not universally required, but widely adopted. The FAA's AC 20-162A describes an accepted means of automated identification of parts using passive UHF RFID, and ATA Spec 2000 Chapter 9-5 codifies the data layout. Boeing, Airbus, Embraer and most Tier-1 airframe and engine OEMs now require RFID on designated part classes (LRUs, rotables, life-limited parts). Defense programs add MIL-STD-130N IUID requirements on top.

faq.question: What chip families does Proud Tek supply for aerospace RFID?
faq.answer: UHF: Impinj M730 / M750 (Monza R6 / R6-P class), NXP UCODE 9 / 9xe, Alien Higgs-9 — mounted on ceramic or PPS on-metal substrates for 30-year airframe life. NFC: NTAG216 / NTAG224 for on-tag lifecycle data (up to 888 bytes); NTAG424 DNA for authenticated part nameplates with SUN codes.

faq.question: Can an aerospace RFID tag survive DO-160G environmental testing?
faq.answer: Yes, when specified correctly. Proud Tek aerospace tags are qualified to DO-160G temperature (-55 to +125 °C), humidity, altitude, vibration, shock, temperature cycling, contamination and RF susceptibility requirements. We provide the full qualification documentation package as part of first-article inspection.

faq.question: How does RFID work for MRO tool control?
faq.answer: Every tool is tagged with a UHF hard tag (Impinj M730 or equivalent). The tool cabinet or shadow board has a fixed UHF reader that inventories the tools continuously. When a mechanic takes a tool, the reader logs it against the mechanic's badge; when the tool returns, the board confirms return. Before a mechanic can sign off their shift or an aircraft can release to service, every tool must be accounted for. Eliminating FOD risk and satisfying FAA Part 145 tool-accountability requirements.

faq.question: What about on-metal UHF tags for Line-Replaceable Units (LRUs)?
faq.answer: LRU housings are metal and require on-metal UHF tags, not paper-substrate labels. Proud Tek supplies ceramic and PPS-substrate UHF tags (Impinj M730 / UCODE 9) with read range 1.5-3 m on metal, ATA-compliant EPC encoding, and a temperature / vibration / humidity profile that matches the LRU's service environment (avionics bay, wheel well, engine nacelle, etc.).
